comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the lowest group was just short of $40K and the highest was about $155K.  I also noticed that the first 4 groups are about what most people would consider basic human needs and/or civil rights topics.  Finally, I noticed that the other topics are all about either mental/emotional stress/struggles or physical stress/struggles.

I wonder what the biggest challenge with travel would be for the highest income group.  I also wonder if the pressures and stresses listed were self-imposed or if they were imposed by others.  Finally, I wonder if there were any students that applied outside of the $40K - $155K range and what their topics were.

I think this relates to me and my community of students because it is helpful for everyone to be aware of the different struggles people face based on their level of income.  Over the years, it has become extremely hard for students to think outside of their own situation, so this graph would help them do that.  It may also help students realize how big of a challenge the question is asking for when they go to write their own college application essays.

The title I would give this graph is: "Life's challenges, by household income, as told by University of California applicants"

comments.raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed, while it is subjective, is that as household income increases the college essay topics become “less serious”. What I mean by this is the difference between the topics of economic insecurity, abuse, and domestic instability falling to households with an income of 65k and under, while topics like travel, sports, and failure fall to households with an income of 125k and over. While looking at the graph, I also noticed that the vast majority of the essay topics had some form of negative connotation. I wonder what percentage of students’ essays that were surveyed for this fell into Other/Miscellaneous categories. I also noticed that the essay topics were gathered for a specific essay prompt that applicants may answer, out of many different options. I wonder how this fact affected the range of essay topics and what the data would look like if it included other prompts. Since this data was compiled for only the University of California applicants, I wonder how this same data breaks down for different schools or even by state.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I noticed that there is a vast difference in incomes when it comes to college essay submissions. The people with the highest income talked about travel, while the people with the lowest tended to talk about economic/material insecurity abuse. I wonder why people who have high incomes tend to talk about traveling a lot. I understand that because they have a high income that they have the money to be able to travel, but there are so many different topics out there. I also notice that the people with the lowest income talk about economic and material insecurity abuse which may be something that they and their families go through in life. The people who make similar incomes tend to talk about very different topics and I wonder why that is. College essays are normally based on real-life experiences that a person has gone through. That is what makes this graph so interesting because it shows how money can affect someone's ideas and beliefs. This relates to me because soon I will be writing my own college essay, and while I have come up with many ideas, it is very interesting to see other people who have a similar financial status to my family put their own spin on their essay. The essay topics are so different so I also wonder what made these certain students decide to write their college essay based on some of these topics. A catchy headline is "Students Take On Their Own College Essay."

The graph is of the relationship between the subject of student essays and the average household income of the students. The subject is in response to the question of what were their most difficult challenges. The subject with the lowest income is economic/material insecurity, and the subject with the highest income is travel. The lowest four subjects are some sort of hardship or difficulty in life. 

I wonder why students considered travel to be challenging, it is an odd one out because all of the other subjects are standard life challenges. I wonder why discrimination is at $100k, I would have expected it to be lower because financial discrimination is a type of discrimination. I wonder why failure is the second highest income.

This impacts me and my community because I am a high school senior. I just wrote a college essay a couple months ago, and the subject of a college essay is a very important choice.

comments.raw_comment:
I would argue that as the average household income increases, the college essays actually become more personal. In a way, topics such as Economic/Material Insecurity, Immigration, Abuse are more about how the outside world affects them, while topics like Failure, Sports, and Relationships are more about their own actions. This could be because many students of higher income are aware of their privilege, and instead of writing about things that were given to them, they write about topics they were more personally involved in. 

I wonder about the distribution of the data, and how many essays were actually written about each subject. I also would want to know how spread out the averages are. For example, do most people who write about academics have an income of around $100k, or is it scattered all throughout the income range?

A good title would be: "The impact of money, and what that could mean for college students."

comments.raw_comment:
One of the things that really interested me was the various demands and problems in relation to the income levels. In lower income essays, they mainly talked about immediate problems that are much more likely to happen when you are poor, like the chances of abuse, hunger, and lack of affordable housing. In middle class essays, they mainly talked about emotional difficulties, which are likely to happen if you're pressured by those around you to rise up the social ladder and become wealthier. And in wealthier families, most of their problems stem from their wealth, like maybe a problem during a vacation or a sports dispute, extras that the other families would be less likely to afford. 

One category that really stuck out to me was discrimination, and how it was firmly in the middle of the income range. I guess maybe when people of color are a part of the middle class, they are likely to live in suburbs, which might be more discrminatory to them. Or, maybe it's because if you're an ambitious woman or POC or both, you might be more likely to encounter bigots who will try to slow you down.

This isn't really answering the questions, but were observations that I made. If there isn't already a title for it, it would be "Money doesn't always buy true happiness"

comments.raw_comment:
A good headline for this graph might be: Wages and Worries.

One of my observations on this is that the graph has lower income families dealing with serious topics, while families with higher incomes deal with less serious topics. One thing I noticed, however, is that the graph doesn't necessarily cover all the incomes. Most of this graph would be working class families, but even on the higher end, that might still only be considered middle class.

I do wonder if there was a reason for choosing the selected categories on this topic for the graph.

This does relate to me and my community due to the fact that everyone in my community has different wages, and each person has their own sets of problems. That, however, doesn't mean people from low or high income families can write about different topics outside of their income. Take for example: A low income family can write about sports, while a student from a high income family can write about death. Everyone in life has problems, it is just that some of those are influenced by the environment.

The more serious responses to personal challenges (economic/material insecurity, abuse, immigration, and death) tend to be from lower-income homes. I was also surprised that discrimination/stereotypes came from relatively higher-income households.

Why did they show the graph the way they did, it could be misleading because it is a list on the side of different subjects in order of income answers with a significant negative slope to income. however, these topics are different and shouldn't look like a comparative slope. It is important to know what kids find as struggles in a community to really find their own privilege... some people wrote about sports and travel while others wrote about abuse and death. This doesn't mean that there isn't abuse in higher-income households in any way but it is a good measure to check your privilege.

comments.raw_comment:
1) I think that the most notable aspect of this graph is the range of topics from more serious issues to essays that showcase positive experiences. I think that this graph further reflects our society at large, and accurately illustrates the hardships of living in a capitalist society and the privileges of the upper-class.

2) As a country that supposedly takes pride in its students, achievements, and academia, why do mere teenagers have to share their hardships as fairy tales, essentially entertaining the college board, to simply take the next step in pursuing knowledge of their choosing? 

3) I think this article relates to my community because many students too feel disdain for the American education system and do hope to see some change. 

4) A large reason I want to go to college is less so that I can continue to educate myself on subjects that I'm passionate about and more-so so that I can “get a degree, a good job, and have an honest income” as we are told to do so. In fact the careers I'm interested in, the majors I wish to pursue, don’t provide enough to live ideally and stably as one would like. I also don’t wish to subject myself to societal labels such as “uneducated” for choosing not to further an education that could potentially strip me of the wealth I'm told to go after.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the relationship between the college essay subjects students chose to answer the prompt “Describe the most significant challenge you have faced and the steps you have taken to overcome this challenge” and their family’s household income. Evidence was gathered in November 2016, before the pandemic, from 60,000 University of California applications.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included thus graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series.
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Jan 7 with moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 12.  The topic – international Covid vaccination rates.  Keep noticing and wondering.

This relates to me because judging by my own community's average household's monthly income, it is possible to estimate what the most common topic for college essays will be for youth.

comments.raw_comment:
From the graph, I noticed that as average reported household income of students increased, the issues they discussed in their essays became more materialistic. For example, students with lower household incomes discussed serious, personal topics like abuse, immigration, and economic insecurity, while students with higher household incomes discussed topics like sports, failure, and travel that was not related to immigration and relocation.
I wonder if students with lower average household incomes discuss mostly serious, personal issues because they were faced with lots of hardship in their lifetime due to their family's income, and are more open considering they likely experienced these hardships for most of their lives. I wonder if the students with higher average household incomes discussed more materialistic issues because they hadn't really been faced with profound, serious hardships due to their economic stability and only really knew materialistic issues in their lifetime.
This relates to me and my community because I am sure we have a wide range of average household incomes even within my school district alone, and our average household income likely impacts the issues we write about in our college essays as well. Our community is very diverse and there is a large disparity between average household incomes, and these two factors likely impact college essay topics used.
"Personal or Material? How Income Impacts College Essay Topics"

comments.raw_comment: In the graph, I realized that as the family income increases, more problems become evident. When at $40k the only problem is economic/material insecurity which is a given as it is small compared to the large sums of money proceeding it. However, as money ranges from $80k to $105k you begin to experience worse issues like death, academics, mental wellness, as well as emotions and relationships. This makes me wonder if having more money is really as good as it seems, as despite having a lot of money seems good due to being able to possess more things you can than if you're poor you lose the satisfaction of work towards gaining your desires. This relates to me and my community because my family and many other families in our town have  relatively stable incomes, however it is obvious that there are still issues present. A catchy headline for this is: "Is Money Really That Good? Let's See what These College Essays Es-Say!"

What do you notice?

In the graph, I noticed that the majority of the kids who the data was taken from, tend to have more serious problems when the household income is lower, and the higher the household income, the nicer things they can relate to. For example, the lowest household income, which is less than 40k a year, writes about economic / material insecurity, while the highest howhold income, which is more than 150k a year, writes about travel experiences. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder where this data was taken from, if it was from a certain town, region, state, college, etc. Was this collection of data biased or unbiased? How many students participated and what was the number of them? Did the students know they were participating?

How does this relate to you and your community?

This relates to me and my community because college essays are going to become very common to my age range, starting next year.

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

A catchy name for this graph's main idea could be, do families and their struggles equal their annual salary?

I also wonder if students who are more economically struggling tend to write more in-depth essays in hopes of gaining higher scholarship grants, while students in wealthier families are not faced with this struggle.

comments.raw_comment:
1) I noticed that the focused issue varied based on the range of average family household income. For example, relatively lower income households, including from about 40k-80k, were more inclined to write about social issues including economic insecurity and immigration. This possibly indicates a glimpse to the personal lives of these students, suggesting a possible correlation between average income and how it effects home life. 

2) I wonder what the relationship is between how much income a family receives and the likelihood of the students in the families to face prominent social issues.  I also wonder if this position almost gives lower-income students an "upper-hand" when applying to colleges because it seems as though admissions officials strive to see more "real-world" personal struggle responses when asked a prompt like this, as compared to an issue not as intense such as sports. 

3) This relates to me and my community because as a high school student I will be writing college essays one day as well. It is interesting to self asses and reflect on how my family's financial situation can effect my perspective on life. 

4)  "See Just How Much Money Effects Your Perspective On Life"

comments.raw_comment:
1) I noticed that college students who have written about serious challenges tend to have a lower family household income compared to college students who have written about secondary/minor challenges. For example, those who have written college essays on Economic/Material Insecurity, Abuse, and Domestic Instability ranged a family household income from approximately $40k to $65k. In contrast, sports, failure, and those who struggle with travelling (unrelated to immigration and relocation) have a household income ranging from approximately $125k to $155k.

2) I wonder if the type of university and family household income impacted the type of essay topic the college students wrote about. Is it possible for college students who have high household incomes to struggle with serious problems? How did they even pick the essays to display the following results>

3) This relates to my community because the variety of household incomes are impacted by the challenges that people face. There are a lot of reasons why someone is able to acquire and obtain the lives they have and the graph displays an example of one of them.

4) My catchy headline for this graph is: "Mo Money, Less Problems."

All of the college essay subjects I was thinking of writing about fall into one of these categories.

1) I notice that college applicants that come from lower income households write about topics that may be more traumatic or have had a negative impact on their lives, such as abuse and economic instability. On the other hand, college applicants coming from higher income households tend to write about topics that are less negative or may not have had a traumatic impact on a student’s life, such as travel and sports.

More specifically, are there any students over a 90k income who chose to write about immigration, or insecurity? A catchy title I would use to name this graph would be something like: "How does the income of students "incompass" the issues they face?"

We notice that this looks more like a table more than a graph. The top part of the graph has average family income per year. We also notice that the data points form a negative line of best fit. What we wonder:

This seems like a graph that is centered around the United States in terms of college admissions (because of the inclusion of the topic of college essays). We wonder how the results would differ if this data was collected from an international scale. We also wonder if international college processes even require essays, making us question if this table would be even relevant in other places.

One catchy title could be:
"From Economic Insecurity to Travel: How Income Effects Essay Topics"

comments.raw_comment:
What do I notice?

I notice that the lower a family’s income, the more likely a student is to discuss financial insecurity, abuse, domestic instability, and immigration in their college essays. The higher a family’s income, the more likely a student is to discuss travel, failure, sports, and emotions.

What do I wonder?

I wonder how income specifically prompts students to discuss certain topics in their college essays. For example, having low income for a family can cause stress on parents and children; never knowing if there will be food on the table can lead to abuse and poor domestic relationships if stress is not dealt with in a healthy way. Perhaps students with low domestic income have immigrants for parents and therefore have less economic opportunity than kids who have native-born parents. On the other hand, students with a higher domestic income probably had a higher education than students with a lower domestic income, as a result, there are higher expectations for those students to succeed, and they probably discuss their fear of failure on their college essays. They have the money to participate in sports and discuss their hardships/ experiences in the game. Maybe they aspire to travel which is something students with lower income couldn’t dream of.

How does this relate to me?

My community for the most part is middle class, so perhaps the hardships we discuss on our college essays will not be about money.

Title: Does Financial Insecurity Lead to Maturity?
